# Frobenius pseudoprime

- [Español](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%BAmero_pseudoprimo_de_Frobenius)
- [Русский](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%9F%D1%81%D0%B5%D0%B2%D0%B4%D0%BE%D0%BF%D1%80%D0%BE%D1%81%D1%82%D0%BE%D0%B5_%D1%87%D0%B8%D1%81%D0%BB%D0%BE_%D0%A4%D1%80%D0%BE%D0%B1%D0%B5%D0%BD%D0%B8%D1%83%D1%81%D0%B0)
 [Edit links](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Special:EntityPage/Q5505102#sitelinks-wikipedia)                          From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia   Type of pseudoprime ![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/f/f2/Edit-clear.svg/40px-Edit-clear.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)This article **may be too technical for most readers to understand**. Please [help improve it](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frobenius_pseudoprime&action=edit) to [make it understandable to non-experts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Make_technical_articles_understandable), without removing the technical details. *(August 2021)**([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance_template_removal))*

In [number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number_theory), a **Frobenius pseudoprime** is a [pseudoprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudoprime), whose definition was inspired by the [quadratic Frobenius test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_Frobenius_test) described by Jon Grantham in a 1998 preprint and published in 2000.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-Grantham98-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-Grantham01-2) Frobenius pseudoprimes can be defined with respect to [polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial) of degree at least 2, but they have been most extensively studied in the case of [quadratic polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_polynomial).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-CP05-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-Loebenberger08-4)

## Frobenius pseudoprimes w.r.t. quadratic polynomials

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frobenius_pseudoprime&action=edit&section=1)]

The definition of Frobenius pseudoprimes with respect to a monic quadratic polynomial      x  2   − P x + Q   {\displaystyle x^{2}-Px+Q}  , where the [discriminant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discriminant)     D =  P  2   − 4 Q   {\displaystyle D=P^{2}-4Q}   is not a square, can be expressed in terms of [Lucas sequences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_sequence)      U  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle U_{n}(P,Q)}   and      V  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,Q)}   as follows.

A [composite number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composite_number) *n* is a Frobenius     ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle (P,Q)}   pseudoprime if and only if

     ( 1 )  gcd ( n , 2 Q D ) = 1 ,   {\displaystyle (1)\qquad \gcd(n,2QD)=1,}       ( 2 )   U  n − δ   ( P , Q ) ≡ 0   ( mod  n )  ,   {\displaystyle (2)\qquad U_{n-\delta }(P,Q)\equiv 0{\pmod {n}},}   and     ( 3 )   V  n − δ   ( P , Q ) ≡ 2  Q  ( 1 − δ )  /  2     ( mod  n )  ,   {\displaystyle (3)\qquad V_{n-\delta }(P,Q)\equiv 2Q^{(1-\delta )/2}{\pmod {n}},}

where     δ =  (    D n    )    {\displaystyle \delta =\left({\tfrac {D}{n}}\right)}   is the [Jacobi symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobi_symbol).

When condition (2) is satisfied, condition (3) becomes equivalent to

     (  3 ′  )   V  n   ( P , Q ) ≡ P   ( mod  n )  .   {\displaystyle (3')\qquad V_{n}(P,Q)\equiv P{\pmod {n}}.}

Therefore, a Frobenius     ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle (P,Q)}   pseudoprime n can be equivalently defined by conditions (1–3), or by conditions (1–2) and (3′).

Since conditions (2) and (3) hold for all primes which satisfy the simple condition (1), they can be used as a [probable primality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probable_prime) test. (If condition (1) fails, then either the [greatest common divisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greatest_common_divisor) is less than n, in which case it is a non-trivial factor and n is composite, or the GCD equals n, in which case one should try different parameters P and Q which are not multiples of n.)

## Relations to other pseudoprimes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frobenius_pseudoprime&action=edit&section=2)]

Every Frobenius     ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle (P,Q)}   pseudoprime is also

- a [Lucas pseudoprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_pseudoprime) with parameters     ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle (P,Q)}  , since it is defined by conditions (1) and (2);[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-Grantham01-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-CP05-3)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-Rotkiewicz03-5)
- a [Dickson pseudoprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dickson_pseudoprime?action=edit&redlink=1) with parameters     ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle (P,Q)}  , since it is defined by conditions (1) and (3');[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-Rotkiewicz03-5)
- a [Fermat pseudoprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime) base      |  Q  |    {\displaystyle |Q|}   when      |  Q  |  > 1   {\displaystyle |Q|>1}  .

The converse of none of these statements is true, making the Frobenius     ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle (P,Q)}   pseudoprimes a proper subset of each of the sets of Lucas pseudoprimes and Dickson pseudoprimes with parameters     ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle (P,Q)}  , and Fermat pseudoprimes to base      |  Q  |    {\displaystyle |Q|}   when      |  Q  |  > 1   {\displaystyle |Q|>1}  . Furthermore, it follows that for the same parameters     ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle (P,Q)}  , a composite number is a Frobenius pseudoprime if and only if it is both a Lucas and Dickson pseudoprime. In other words, for every fixed pair of parameters     ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle (P,Q)}  , the set of Frobenius pseudoprimes equals the intersection of the sets of Lucas and Dickson pseudoprimes.

While each Frobenius     ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle (P,Q)}   pseudoprime is a Lucas pseudoprime, it is not necessarily a [strong Lucas pseudoprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_pseudoprime#Strong_Lucas_pseudoprimes). For example, 6721 is the first Frobenius pseudoprime for     ( P , Q ) = ( 1 , − 1 )   {\displaystyle (P,Q)=(1,-1)}  , which is not a strong Lucas pseudoprime.

Every Frobenius pseudoprime to      x  3   − x − 1   {\displaystyle x^{3}-x-1}   is also a [restricted Perrin pseudoprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perrin_number#Perrin_primality_test). Analogous statements hold for other cubic polynomials of the form      x  3   − r  x  2   + s x − 1   {\displaystyle x^{3}-rx^{2}+sx-1}  .[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-Grantham01-2)

## Examples

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frobenius_pseudoprime&action=edit&section=3)]

Frobenius pseudoprimes with respect to the Fibonacci polynomial      x  2   − x − 1   {\displaystyle x^{2}-x-1}   are determined in terms of the [Fibonacci numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibonacci_numbers)      F  n   =  U  n   ( 1 , − 1 )   {\displaystyle F_{n}=U_{n}(1,-1)}   and [Lucas numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_numbers)      L  n   =  V  n   ( 1 , − 1 )   {\displaystyle L_{n}=V_{n}(1,-1)}  . Such Frobenius pseudoprimes form the sequence:

 4181, 5777, 6721, 10877, 13201, 15251, 34561, 51841, 64079, 64681, 67861, 68251, 75077, 90061, 96049, 97921, 100127, 113573, 118441, 146611, 161027, 162133, 163081, 186961, 197209, 219781, 231703, 252601, 254321, 257761, 268801, 272611, 283361, 302101, 303101, 330929, 399001, 430127, 433621, 438751, 489601, ... (sequence [A212424](https://oeis.org/A212424) in the [OEIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On-Line_Encyclopedia_of_Integer_Sequences)).

While 323 is the first [Lucas pseudoprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_pseudoprime) with respect to the Fibonacci polynomial      x  2   − x − 1   {\displaystyle x^{2}-x-1}  , the first Frobenius pseudoprime with respect to the same polynomial is 4181 (Grantham stated it as 5777[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-Grantham01-2) but multiple authors have noted this is incorrect and is instead the first pseudoprime with      (    5 n    )  = − 1   {\displaystyle \left({\tfrac {5}{n}}\right)=-1}   for this polynomial[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-CP05-3)).

Another case, Frobenius pseudoprimes with respect to the quadratic polynomial      x  2   − 3 x − 1   {\displaystyle x^{2}-3x-1}   can be determined using the Lucas     ( 3 , − 1 )   {\displaystyle (3,-1)}   sequence and are:

 119, 649, 1189, 4187, 12871, 14041, 16109, 23479, 24769, 28421, 31631, 34997, 38503, 41441, 48577, 50545, 56279, 58081, 59081, 61447, 75077, 91187, 95761, 96139, 116821, 127937, 146329, 148943, 150281, 157693, 170039, 180517, 188501, 207761, 208349, 244649, 281017, 311579, 316409, 349441, 350173, 363091, 371399, 397927, 423721, 440833, 459191, 473801, 479119, 493697, ... (sequence [A327655](https://oeis.org/A327655) in the [OEIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On-Line_Encyclopedia_of_Integer_Sequences))

In this case, the first Frobenius pseudoprime with respect to the quadratic polynomial      x  2   − 3 x − 1   {\displaystyle x^{2}-3x-1}   is 119, which is also the first Lucas pseudoprime with respect to the same polynomial. Besides,      (    13 119    )  = − 1   {\displaystyle \left({\tfrac {13}{119}}\right)=-1}  .

The quadratic polynomial      x  2   − 3 x − 5   {\displaystyle x^{2}-3x-5}  , i.e.     ( P , Q ) = ( 3 , − 5 )   {\displaystyle (P,Q)=(3,-5)}  , has sparser pseudoprimes as compared to many other simple quadratics. Using the same process as above, we get the sequence:

 13333, 44801, 486157, 1615681, 3125281, 4219129, 9006401, 12589081, 13404751, 15576571, 16719781, ….

Notice there are only 3 such pseudoprimes below 500,000, while there are many Frobenius (1, −1) and (3, −1) pseudoprimes below 500,000.

Every entry in this sequence is a [Fermat pseudoprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime) to base 5 as well as a Lucas (3, −5) pseudoprime, but the converse is not true: 642,001 is both a psp-5 and a Lucas (3,−5) pseudoprime, but is not a Frobenius (3, −5) pseudoprime. (Note that [Lucas pseudoprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_pseudoprime) for a (*P*, *Q*) pair need not to be a [Fermat pseudoprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime) for base |*Q*|, e.g. 14209 is a Lucas (1, −3) pseudoprime, but not a Fermat pseudoprime for base 3.)

## Strong Frobenius pseudoprimes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frobenius_pseudoprime&action=edit&section=4)]

Strong Frobenius pseudoprimes are also defined.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-Grantham01-2) Details on implementation for quadratic polynomials can be found in Crandall and Pomerance.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-CP05-3)

By imposing the restrictions that     δ = − 1   {\displaystyle \delta =-1}   and     Q ≠ ± 1   {\displaystyle Q\neq \pm 1}  , the authors of [[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-6) show how to choose     P   {\displaystyle P}   and     Q   {\displaystyle Q}   such that there are only *five* odd, composite numbers less than      10  15     {\displaystyle 10^{15}}   for which (3) holds, that is, for which      V  n + 1   ≡ 2 Q   ( mod  n )    {\displaystyle V_{n+1}\equiv 2Q{\pmod {n}}}  .

## Pseudoprimality tests

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frobenius_pseudoprime&action=edit&section=5)]

The conditions defining Frobenius pseudoprime can be used for testing a given number *n* for [probable primality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probable_prime). Often such tests do not rely on fixed parameters     ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle (P,Q)}  , but rather select them in a certain way depending on the input number *n* in order to decrease the proportion of [false positives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_positive), i.e., composite numbers that pass the test. Sometimes such composite numbers are commonly called Frobenius pseudoprimes, although they may correspond to different parameters.

Using parameter selection ideas first laid out in Baillie and Wagstaff (1980)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-lpsp-7) as part of the [Baillie–PSW primality test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baillie%E2%80%93PSW_primality_test) and used by Grantham in his [quadratic Frobenius test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_Frobenius_test),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-QFT-8) one can create even better quadratic tests. In particular, it was shown that choosing parameters from [quadratic non-residues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_non-residue) modulo *n* (based on the [Jacobi symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobi_symbol)) makes far stronger tests, and is one reason for the success of the [Baillie–PSW primality test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baillie%E2%80%93PSW_primality_test). For instance, for the parameters (*P*,2), where *P* is the first odd integer that satisfies      (    D n    )  = − 1   {\displaystyle \left({\tfrac {D}{n}}\right)=-1}  , there are no pseudoprimes below 264.

Yet another test is proposed by Khashin.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-Khashin13-9) For a given [non-square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_number) number *n*, it first computes a parameter *c* as the smallest odd prime having Jacobi symbol      (    c n    )  = − 1   {\displaystyle \left({\tfrac {c}{n}}\right)=-1}  , and then verifies the congruence:

     ( 1 +   c    )  n   ≡ ( 1 −   c   )   ( mod  n )    {\displaystyle (1+{\sqrt {c}})^{n}\equiv (1-{\sqrt {c}}){\pmod {n}}}  .

While all prime *n* pass this test, a composite *n* passes it if and only if *n* is a Frobenius pseudoprime for     ( P , Q ) = ( 2 , 1 − c )   {\displaystyle (P,Q)=(2,1-c)}  . Similar to the above example, Khashin notes that no pseudoprime has been found for his test. He further shows that any that exist under 260 must have a factor less than 19 or have *c* > 128.

### Properties

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frobenius_pseudoprime&action=edit&section=6)]

The computational cost of the Frobenius pseudoprimality test with respect to quadratic polynomials is roughly three times the cost of a [strong pseudoprimality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_pseudoprime) test (i.e. a single round of the [Miller–Rabin primality test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miller%E2%80%93Rabin_primality_test)), 1.5 times that of a [Lucas pseudoprimality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_pseudoprime) test, and slightly more than a [Baillie–PSW primality test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baillie%E2%80%93PSW_primality_test).

Note that the quadratic Frobenius test is stronger than the Lucas test. For example, 1763 is a Lucas pseudoprime to (*P*, *Q*) = (3, −1) since *U*1764(3,−1) ≡ 0 (mod 1763) (*U*(3,−1) is given in (sequence [A006190](https://oeis.org/A006190) in the [OEIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On-Line_Encyclopedia_of_Integer_Sequences))), and it also passes the Jacobi step since      (    13 1763    )  = − 1   {\displaystyle \left({\tfrac {13}{1763}}\right)=-1}  , but it fails the Frobenius test to *x*2 − 3*x* − 1. This property can be clearly seen when the algorithm is formulated as shown in Crandall and Pomerance Algorithm 3.6.9[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-CP05-3) or as shown by Loebenberger,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-Loebenberger08-4) as the algorithm does a Lucas test followed by an additional check for the Frobenius condition.

While the quadratic Frobenius test does not have formal error bounds beyond that of the Lucas test, it can be used as the basis for methods with much smaller error bounds. Note that these have more steps, additional requirements, and non-negligible additional computation beyond what is described on this page. The error bounds for these methods **do not apply** to the standard or strong Frobenius tests with fixed values of (P,Q) described on this page.

Based on this idea of pseudoprimes, algorithms with strong worst-case error bounds can be built. The [quadratic Frobenius test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_Frobenius_test),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-QFT-8) using a quadratic Frobenius test plus other conditions, has a bound of        1 7710      {\displaystyle {\tfrac {1}{7710}}}  . Müller in 2001 proposed the MQFT test with bounds of essentially        1  131040  t        {\displaystyle {\tfrac {1}{131040^{t}}}}  .[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-10) Damgård and Frandsen in 2003 proposed the EQFT with a bound of essentially        256   331776   t        {\displaystyle {\tfrac {256}{{331776}^{t}}}}  .[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-11) Seysen in 2005 proposed the SQFT test with a bound of        1   4096   t        {\displaystyle {\tfrac {1}{{4096}^{t}}}}   and a SQFT3 test with a bound of        16  336442  t        {\displaystyle {\tfrac {16}{336442^{t}}}}  .[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-12)

Given the same computational effort, these offer better worst-case bounds than the commonly used [Miller–Rabin primality test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miller%E2%80%93Rabin_primality_test).

# Frobenius pseudoprime

- [Español](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%BAmero_pseudoprimo_de_Frobenius)

In [number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number_theory), a **Frobenius pseudoprime** is a [pseudoprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudoprime), whose definition was inspired by the [quadratic Frobenius test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_Frobenius_test) described by Jon Grantham in a 1998 preprint and published in 2000.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-Grantham98-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-Grantham01-2) Frobenius pseudoprimes can be defined with respect to [polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial) of degree at least 2, but they have been most extensively studied in the case of [quadratic polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_polynomial).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-CP05-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-Loebenberger08-4)

Frobenius pseudoprimes w.r.t. quadratic polynomials

# Frobenius pseudoprimes w.r.t. quadratic polynomials

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frobenius_pseudoprime&action=edit&section=1)]

The definition of Frobenius pseudoprimes with respect to a monic quadratic polynomial      x  2   − P x + Q   {\displaystyle x^{2}-Px+Q}  , where the [discriminant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discriminant)     D =  P  2   − 4 Q   {\displaystyle D=P^{2}-4Q}   is not a square, can be expressed in terms of [Lucas sequences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_sequence)      U  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle U_{n}(P,Q)}   and      V  n   ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle V_{n}(P,Q)}   as follows.

A [composite number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composite_number) *n* is a Frobenius     ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle (P,Q)}   pseudoprime if and only if

     ( 1 )  gcd ( n , 2 Q D ) = 1 ,   {\displaystyle (1)\qquad \gcd(n,2QD)=1,}       ( 2 )   U  n − δ   ( P , Q ) ≡ 0   ( mod  n )  ,   {\displaystyle (2)\qquad U_{n-\delta }(P,Q)\equiv 0{\pmod {n}},}   and     ( 3 )   V  n − δ   ( P , Q ) ≡ 2  Q  ( 1 − δ )  /  2     ( mod  n )  ,   {\displaystyle (3)\qquad V_{n-\delta }(P,Q)\equiv 2Q^{(1-\delta )/2}{\pmod {n}},}

where     δ =  (    D n    )    {\displaystyle \delta =\left({\tfrac {D}{n}}\right)}   is the [Jacobi symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobi_symbol).

When condition (2) is satisfied, condition (3) becomes equivalent to

     (  3 ′  )   V  n   ( P , Q ) ≡ P   ( mod  n )  .   {\displaystyle (3')\qquad V_{n}(P,Q)\equiv P{\pmod {n}}.}

Therefore, a Frobenius     ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle (P,Q)}   pseudoprime n can be equivalently defined by conditions (1–3), or by conditions (1–2) and (3′).

Since conditions (2) and (3) hold for all primes which satisfy the simple condition (1), they can be used as a [probable primality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probable_prime) test. (If condition (1) fails, then either the [greatest common divisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greatest_common_divisor) is less than n, in which case it is a non-trivial factor and n is composite, or the GCD equals n, in which case one should try different parameters P and Q which are not multiples of n.)

Relations to other pseudoprimes

# Relations to other pseudoprimes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frobenius_pseudoprime&action=edit&section=2)]

Every Frobenius     ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle (P,Q)}   pseudoprime is also

- a [Lucas pseudoprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_pseudoprime) with parameters     ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle (P,Q)}  , since it is defined by conditions (1) and (2);[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-Grantham01-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-CP05-3)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-Rotkiewicz03-5)
- a [Dickson pseudoprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dickson_pseudoprime?action=edit&redlink=1) with parameters     ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle (P,Q)}  , since it is defined by conditions (1) and (3');[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-Rotkiewicz03-5)
- a [Fermat pseudoprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime) base      |  Q  |    {\displaystyle |Q|}   when      |  Q  |  > 1   {\displaystyle |Q|>1}  .

The converse of none of these statements is true, making the Frobenius     ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle (P,Q)}   pseudoprimes a proper subset of each of the sets of Lucas pseudoprimes and Dickson pseudoprimes with parameters     ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle (P,Q)}  , and Fermat pseudoprimes to base      |  Q  |    {\displaystyle |Q|}   when      |  Q  |  > 1   {\displaystyle |Q|>1}  . Furthermore, it follows that for the same parameters     ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle (P,Q)}  , a composite number is a Frobenius pseudoprime if and only if it is both a Lucas and Dickson pseudoprime. In other words, for every fixed pair of parameters     ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle (P,Q)}  , the set of Frobenius pseudoprimes equals the intersection of the sets of Lucas and Dickson pseudoprimes.

While each Frobenius     ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle (P,Q)}   pseudoprime is a Lucas pseudoprime, it is not necessarily a [strong Lucas pseudoprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_pseudoprime#Strong_Lucas_pseudoprimes). For example, 6721 is the first Frobenius pseudoprime for     ( P , Q ) = ( 1 , − 1 )   {\displaystyle (P,Q)=(1,-1)}  , which is not a strong Lucas pseudoprime.

Every Frobenius pseudoprime to      x  3   − x − 1   {\displaystyle x^{3}-x-1}   is also a [restricted Perrin pseudoprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perrin_number#Perrin_primality_test). Analogous statements hold for other cubic polynomials of the form      x  3   − r  x  2   + s x − 1   {\displaystyle x^{3}-rx^{2}+sx-1}  .[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-Grantham01-2)

Examples

# Examples

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frobenius_pseudoprime&action=edit&section=3)]

Frobenius pseudoprimes with respect to the Fibonacci polynomial      x  2   − x − 1   {\displaystyle x^{2}-x-1}   are determined in terms of the [Fibonacci numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibonacci_numbers)      F  n   =  U  n   ( 1 , − 1 )   {\displaystyle F_{n}=U_{n}(1,-1)}   and [Lucas numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_numbers)      L  n   =  V  n   ( 1 , − 1 )   {\displaystyle L_{n}=V_{n}(1,-1)}  . Such Frobenius pseudoprimes form the sequence:

 4181, 5777, 6721, 10877, 13201, 15251, 34561, 51841, 64079, 64681, 67861, 68251, 75077, 90061, 96049, 97921, 100127, 113573, 118441, 146611, 161027, 162133, 163081, 186961, 197209, 219781, 231703, 252601, 254321, 257761, 268801, 272611, 283361, 302101, 303101, 330929, 399001, 430127, 433621, 438751, 489601, ... (sequence [A212424](https://oeis.org/A212424) in the [OEIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On-Line_Encyclopedia_of_Integer_Sequences)).

While 323 is the first [Lucas pseudoprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_pseudoprime) with respect to the Fibonacci polynomial      x  2   − x − 1   {\displaystyle x^{2}-x-1}  , the first Frobenius pseudoprime with respect to the same polynomial is 4181 (Grantham stated it as 5777[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-Grantham01-2) but multiple authors have noted this is incorrect and is instead the first pseudoprime with      (    5 n    )  = − 1   {\displaystyle \left({\tfrac {5}{n}}\right)=-1}   for this polynomial[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-CP05-3)).

Another case, Frobenius pseudoprimes with respect to the quadratic polynomial      x  2   − 3 x − 1   {\displaystyle x^{2}-3x-1}   can be determined using the Lucas     ( 3 , − 1 )   {\displaystyle (3,-1)}   sequence and are:

 119, 649, 1189, 4187, 12871, 14041, 16109, 23479, 24769, 28421, 31631, 34997, 38503, 41441, 48577, 50545, 56279, 58081, 59081, 61447, 75077, 91187, 95761, 96139, 116821, 127937, 146329, 148943, 150281, 157693, 170039, 180517, 188501, 207761, 208349, 244649, 281017, 311579, 316409, 349441, 350173, 363091, 371399, 397927, 423721, 440833, 459191, 473801, 479119, 493697, ... (sequence [A327655](https://oeis.org/A327655) in the [OEIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On-Line_Encyclopedia_of_Integer_Sequences))

In this case, the first Frobenius pseudoprime with respect to the quadratic polynomial      x  2   − 3 x − 1   {\displaystyle x^{2}-3x-1}   is 119, which is also the first Lucas pseudoprime with respect to the same polynomial. Besides,      (    13 119    )  = − 1   {\displaystyle \left({\tfrac {13}{119}}\right)=-1}  .

The quadratic polynomial      x  2   − 3 x − 5   {\displaystyle x^{2}-3x-5}  , i.e.     ( P , Q ) = ( 3 , − 5 )   {\displaystyle (P,Q)=(3,-5)}  , has sparser pseudoprimes as compared to many other simple quadratics. Using the same process as above, we get the sequence:

 13333, 44801, 486157, 1615681, 3125281, 4219129, 9006401, 12589081, 13404751, 15576571, 16719781, ….

Notice there are only 3 such pseudoprimes below 500,000, while there are many Frobenius (1, −1) and (3, −1) pseudoprimes below 500,000.

Every entry in this sequence is a [Fermat pseudoprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime) to base 5 as well as a Lucas (3, −5) pseudoprime, but the converse is not true: 642,001 is both a psp-5 and a Lucas (3,−5) pseudoprime, but is not a Frobenius (3, −5) pseudoprime. (Note that [Lucas pseudoprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_pseudoprime) for a (*P*, *Q*) pair need not to be a [Fermat pseudoprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime) for base |*Q*|, e.g. 14209 is a Lucas (1, −3) pseudoprime, but not a Fermat pseudoprime for base 3.)

Strong Frobenius pseudoprimes

# Strong Frobenius pseudoprimes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frobenius_pseudoprime&action=edit&section=4)]

Strong Frobenius pseudoprimes are also defined.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-Grantham01-2) Details on implementation for quadratic polynomials can be found in Crandall and Pomerance.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-CP05-3)

By imposing the restrictions that     δ = − 1   {\displaystyle \delta =-1}   and     Q ≠ ± 1   {\displaystyle Q\neq \pm 1}  , the authors of [[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-6) show how to choose     P   {\displaystyle P}   and     Q   {\displaystyle Q}   such that there are only *five* odd, composite numbers less than      10  15     {\displaystyle 10^{15}}   for which (3) holds, that is, for which      V  n + 1   ≡ 2 Q   ( mod  n )    {\displaystyle V_{n+1}\equiv 2Q{\pmod {n}}}  .

Pseudoprimality tests

# Pseudoprimality tests

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frobenius_pseudoprime&action=edit&section=5)]

The conditions defining Frobenius pseudoprime can be used for testing a given number *n* for [probable primality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probable_prime). Often such tests do not rely on fixed parameters     ( P , Q )   {\displaystyle (P,Q)}  , but rather select them in a certain way depending on the input number *n* in order to decrease the proportion of [false positives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_positive), i.e., composite numbers that pass the test. Sometimes such composite numbers are commonly called Frobenius pseudoprimes, although they may correspond to different parameters.

Using parameter selection ideas first laid out in Baillie and Wagstaff (1980)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-lpsp-7) as part of the [Baillie–PSW primality test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baillie%E2%80%93PSW_primality_test) and used by Grantham in his [quadratic Frobenius test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_Frobenius_test),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-QFT-8) one can create even better quadratic tests. In particular, it was shown that choosing parameters from [quadratic non-residues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_non-residue) modulo *n* (based on the [Jacobi symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobi_symbol)) makes far stronger tests, and is one reason for the success of the [Baillie–PSW primality test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baillie%E2%80%93PSW_primality_test). For instance, for the parameters (*P*,2), where *P* is the first odd integer that satisfies      (    D n    )  = − 1   {\displaystyle \left({\tfrac {D}{n}}\right)=-1}  , there are no pseudoprimes below 264.

Yet another test is proposed by Khashin.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-Khashin13-9) For a given [non-square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_number) number *n*, it first computes a parameter *c* as the smallest odd prime having Jacobi symbol      (    c n    )  = − 1   {\displaystyle \left({\tfrac {c}{n}}\right)=-1}  , and then verifies the congruence:

     ( 1 +   c    )  n   ≡ ( 1 −   c   )   ( mod  n )    {\displaystyle (1+{\sqrt {c}})^{n}\equiv (1-{\sqrt {c}}){\pmod {n}}}  .

While all prime *n* pass this test, a composite *n* passes it if and only if *n* is a Frobenius pseudoprime for     ( P , Q ) = ( 2 , 1 − c )   {\displaystyle (P,Q)=(2,1-c)}  . Similar to the above example, Khashin notes that no pseudoprime has been found for his test. He further shows that any that exist under 260 must have a factor less than 19 or have *c* > 128.

Properties

# Properties

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frobenius_pseudoprime&action=edit&section=6)]

The computational cost of the Frobenius pseudoprimality test with respect to quadratic polynomials is roughly three times the cost of a [strong pseudoprimality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_pseudoprime) test (i.e. a single round of the [Miller–Rabin primality test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miller%E2%80%93Rabin_primality_test)), 1.5 times that of a [Lucas pseudoprimality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_pseudoprime) test, and slightly more than a [Baillie–PSW primality test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baillie%E2%80%93PSW_primality_test).

Note that the quadratic Frobenius test is stronger than the Lucas test. For example, 1763 is a Lucas pseudoprime to (*P*, *Q*) = (3, −1) since *U*1764(3,−1) ≡ 0 (mod 1763) (*U*(3,−1) is given in (sequence [A006190](https://oeis.org/A006190) in the [OEIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On-Line_Encyclopedia_of_Integer_Sequences))), and it also passes the Jacobi step since      (    13 1763    )  = − 1   {\displaystyle \left({\tfrac {13}{1763}}\right)=-1}  , but it fails the Frobenius test to *x*2 − 3*x* − 1. This property can be clearly seen when the algorithm is formulated as shown in Crandall and Pomerance Algorithm 3.6.9[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-CP05-3) or as shown by Loebenberger,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-Loebenberger08-4) as the algorithm does a Lucas test followed by an additional check for the Frobenius condition.

While the quadratic Frobenius test does not have formal error bounds beyond that of the Lucas test, it can be used as the basis for methods with much smaller error bounds. Note that these have more steps, additional requirements, and non-negligible additional computation beyond what is described on this page. The error bounds for these methods **do not apply** to the standard or strong Frobenius tests with fixed values of (P,Q) described on this page.

Based on this idea of pseudoprimes, algorithms with strong worst-case error bounds can be built. The [quadratic Frobenius test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_Frobenius_test),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-QFT-8) using a quadratic Frobenius test plus other conditions, has a bound of        1 7710      {\displaystyle {\tfrac {1}{7710}}}  . Müller in 2001 proposed the MQFT test with bounds of essentially        1  131040  t        {\displaystyle {\tfrac {1}{131040^{t}}}}  .[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-10) Damgård and Frandsen in 2003 proposed the EQFT with a bound of essentially        256   331776   t        {\displaystyle {\tfrac {256}{{331776}^{t}}}}  .[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-11) Seysen in 2005 proposed the SQFT test with a bound of        1   4096   t        {\displaystyle {\tfrac {1}{{4096}^{t}}}}   and a SQFT3 test with a bound of        16  336442  t        {\displaystyle {\tfrac {16}{336442^{t}}}}  .[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frobenius_pseudoprime#cite_note-12)

Given the same computational effort, these offer better worst-case bounds than the commonly used [Miller–Rabin primality test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miller%E2%80%93Rabin_primality_test).
